Chapter 5: The Practice of Doing One’s Best in Every Moment
Every new day throws us a different set of challenges—some are tiny and barely noticeable, while others feel completely overwhelming.
Have you ever noticed how some mornings, you wake up full of energy, ready to take on anything? And then there are those other days, where even the smallest tasks seem impossible.
Most of us are really tough on ourselves. We expect perfection, no matter what’s going on. And when we fall short, that inner critic jumps right in—whispering, “You should’ve done better.”
But here’s the truth: nobody can give more than their best in any moment. And what “best” looks like? Well, it changes all the time.
On a really good day, your best might mean powering through a big project with focus and energy. On a tough day, it could simply mean getting out of bed and giving life a shot.
Let me share a story. There’s a parent juggling work, family, and personal struggles. Some days, she managed to cook dinner, help the kids with homework, maybe even squeeze in a little time for herself.
On other days? She ordered takeout and let the kids watch TV. And for years, she felt guilty about those hard days—believing she was somehow failing.
But over time, something shifted. She realized her best was different every day, depending on what life threw at her. The guilt started to fade, replaced by a quiet pride in simply showing up, even when things were tough.
Doing your best isn’t about being perfect. It’s about effort, intention, and a little self-compassion. It means being present and giving what you can, no matter what that looks like on any given day.
It’s letting go of the urge to compare today’s effort to yesterday’s—or to anyone else’s, for that matter. And it’s understanding that rest and recovery are just as important as the things you accomplish.
Most of us are taught to push ourselves, to always strive for more, to never feel satisfied. That drive can be helpful, but if we’re not careful, it turns into a recipe for suffering.
Because when perfection is the only standard, nothing ever feels good enough. That just leads to burnout, frustration, and feeling like you never measure up.
But what if you made a different choice? What if you chose to do your best, and accepted that your best will look different every day? That’s a real act of kindness toward yourself.
It gives you space to grow, to learn, and to actually enjoy the process.
Here’s the thing—when mistakes happen, and they always do, you’ll have room to learn, instead of just judging yourself.
And this practice doesn’t just change your relationship with yourself. It totally shifts the way you relate to others, too.
When you really understand that everyone’s doing the best they can with what they have, it’s so much easier to offer compassion and patience.
Suddenly, relationships become less about blame, and more about support.
In the long run, making a habit of doing your best builds real freedom. It breaks that cycle of harsh self-judgment and opens the door to self-acceptance.
Life starts to feel less about chasing impossible standards, and more about living with integrity and presence.
